description:
We are SixSevenSquad, a student tech team from Pavlodar, Kazakhstan, passionate about software development and space exploration.

For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we aim to build an interactive web tool using NASA data to compare lunar landing sites, visualize Sun and Earth positions, and assess lighting and communication conditions.

Our interests include coding, data analysis, UI/UX design, and scientific visualization.
summary: Lunar Window helps mission planners choose where and when to land on the Moon. For any landing site and date, it answers two questions a lander's survival depends on: will its solar panels see the Sun, and will its antenna still see Earth? Using real NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides and LRO LOLA terrain horizons, it simulates hour by hour the Sun and Earth elevation, sunlight, direct-to-Earth link and battery charge, then gives a clear verdict ("Good window" / "Risky window"). Users can play the timeline, jump to the next sunset to see whether the battery survives the night, compare all 19 catalogue sites on one date, run an optimizer that ranks sites against their requirements and explains why each fails, check real LOLA slopes, and ask an AI Mission Advisor that runs the real calculation engine and explains the result. A 3D scene shows the Moon, Sun, Earth and a full launch-to-touchdown mission. This turns complex orbital geometry into decisions anyone can understand, which matters for Artemis-era south-pole missions, where long shadows and Earth visibility decide success.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Window is a web app for planning lunar landings around two survival constraints: sunlight for power and line of sight to Earth for communication.

1. Pick a site (19 catalogue sites: Apollo, Artemis III south-pole candidates, CLPS, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e) or custom coordinates, a date, a duration and a lander (panels, battery, load).

2. The engine computes Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation for every 30 minutes from NASA JPL Horizons, compares them with the real local horizon (LRO LOLA profiles), and runs an energy balance for the battery.

3. The result is a verdict, telemetry (time in sunlight, longest shadow, link outages, minimum charge) and a timeline you can play hour by hour.

KEY FEATURES

- 3D Moon with the real Sun and Earth directions for the chosen site and time.

- Find sunset: extends the run to 30 days and shows whether the battery survives the night (Energy flow view).

- Compare: all sites side by side on the same date.

- Optimizer: ranks sites against sunlight, Earth-link and battery requirements and explains why each one fails.

- Landing safety: real LOLA 5 m/px slopes (Site04) with an adjustable slope limit.

- NASA terrain layers: global LOLA elevation and slope overlays.

- AI Mission Advisor: Gemini turns a question into one of six validated actions (assess, optimize, compare, delay, alternatives, help); the backend runs the real engine, and all numbers come from the engine, not from the model.

- Full 3D mission: launch, translunar coast, braking and touchdown.

- English and Russian interface, light and dark themes.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

At the lunar south pole the Sun stays near the horizon, so a few degrees of terrain decide whether a lander lives or dies. Example from our data: Malapert massif looks sunny (79.9% of 30 days in sunlight), but one shadow lasts 145 hours and drains the battery to 0%. Lunar Window makes such risks visible in seconds, for mission designers, students and the public.

VALIDATION

Results are checked against independent Horizons tables for Apollo 11, Apollo 17 and Shackleton within 0.02°. Automated tests cover parsing, geometry, energy balance, API flows and the 3D flight path (backend 55 tests, flight 21, UI 14).

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Three.js / React Three Fiber, Zustand, Recharts, Vite; Python FastAPI backend; Docker; Google Gemini API; Remotion for the demo video.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a static table, the app tells the story of a mission: you watch the Sun set behind real lunar terrain, the battery drain, and then fly the mission to the chosen site.
